newsitem.title: USA: Doctors sue U.S. officials over marijuana stance.
newsitem.headline: Doctors sue U.S. officials over marijuana stance.

text.p: A group of California doctors and patients sued U.S. officials Tuesday to prevent them from punishing doctors who recommend their patients use marijuana to cope with AIDS, cancer or glaucoma.
California voters passed a controversial measure last November making it legal for sick people to grow and possess marijuana for medical use when recommended by a doctor.

But the Clinton administration said in December that marijuana remained illegal under federal law and pledged to sanction doctors who prescribed marijuana under the California measure and a similar measure in Arizona.

Retired Gen. Barry McCaffrey, director of the White House Office of National Drug Control Policy, said then that doctors prescribing the drug could face revocation of their practitioner's registration or prosecution.

A group of California doctors, mostly AIDS and cancer specialists, and several patients suffering from AIDS, cancer or epilepsy, filed suit in U.S. District Court in San Francisco, alleging the administration's position violated their First Amendment free speech rights.

"The government is entitled to its opinion. What it is not entitled to is to use threats and intimidation to silence those who disagree with it," Ann Brick, an American Civil Liberties Union attorney representing the plaintiffs, told a news conference.

Virginia Cafaro, a San Francisco doctor who treats AIDS patients, said she felt as if the war on drugs had become the war on physicians. "And I feel like I'm going to be one of the casualties of that war," she said.

The suit said what it called the government's threats were "having their intended effect." Many doctors in California had censored the medical advice they offered to patients and were refusing to give guidance on the risks or benefits of medical marijuana, the lawsuit said.
It said that by "effectively gagging physicians," the government had intruded into the doctor-patient relationship and undermined patients' confidence in their doctors.

Supporters of medical marijuana says the drug often eases nausea in cancer patients undergoing chemotherapy, reduces the pain of AIDS patients and lowers eye pressure in glaucoma sufferers. Opponents, however, painted the California measure as an attempt to legalise marijuana through the back door.
The class-action suit names as defendants McCaffrey, Drug Enforcement Administration chief Thomas Constantine, Attorney General Janet Reno and Health and Human Services Secretary Donna Shalala.

It seeks a court order barring the government from punishing doctors for talking with their patients about the medical use of marijuana or recommending its use. It seeks a declaration that the government's pledge to punish doctors violates the doctors' First Amendment rights.
The Office of National Drug Control Policy said it could not comment on the lawsuit in detail. But it said the government would enforce federal law.

"The aim of the administration's policy is to ensure that no American gets the wrong message about the dangers of drugs and to ensure the safety and efficacy of all medicines available to the American public," it said in a statement.
Justice Department spokesman Gregory King said the department had not yet seen the lawsuit. "We will review it and take appropriate action," he said.
